text.p: On overnight commodity markets copper prices bounced back in London after an early dive on an inventory increase, closing up US$19 a tonne on the day.
Gold prices edged lower again overnight and continue to lanquish below US$340 an ounce despite news of sharper than expected U.S. GDP growth overnight.
Oil prices ended lower after a Venezuelan official spoke about change in the OPEC organisation.
The CRB Index was up 1.61 points at 248.29 at 7.40 a.m. AEDT (2140 GMT).
Copper prices charged higher during late Wednesday LME trading, erasing morning losses and coming within a a whisker of clearing $2,380 per tonne.

Traders said the smart bounce from an early low of $2,325 was a clear example of the market's present volatility and susceptibility to sudden movements in the spread. Backwardations widened out this afternoon, while buy-stops and local speculators kicked in above $2,350.
Others said the short-term fundamentals of strike action in Chile at Escondida, with another strike vote taking place later on Wednesday at Quebrada Blanca, stemmed further declines.
Meanwhile, the spreads tightened up, with some talk that stocks would be lower again on Thursday after today's 2,675 tonne increase in inventories which was the first since February.
The cash/threes backwardation, which narrowed to under $60 at one stage on Wednesday, was back around $88 by the close, albeit a long way off Monday's high water-mark of $210.
Three months prices closed at $2,379, up $19 a tonne from the previous day's kerb.
Elsewhere, the rest of the metals complex grabbed copper's coat tails and advanced during the latter part of the day, although only aluminium saw reasonable activity, they said.
Aluminium managed to climb above stubborn resistance around $1,640 during the kerb, and the current steady upside progress is construed technically constructive. Final trade was at $1,645, up $7.50.
Nickel prices extended an earlier uptick during the kerb, with some chart-based buying kicking in due to a confirmed break above $7,300. Last business was at $7,380, up $100.
Lead and zinc both notched up reasonable advances during the kerb also, with the former metal arresting a slide that left it at at 18-month lows on Tuesday.
Zinc avoided a test of a downside gap, and broke back above $1,270 instead to conclude the day at $1,273, up $8 from the previous kerb.

COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended mostly lower Wednesday, with the exception of silver, after the complex firmed early in the session on the back of a sharp rise in U.S. first quarter GDP. COMEX June gold ended down 40 cents at $341.20, after slipping back from early session highs at $343.20. In the bullion market spot gold ended quoted $339.30/80, compared to the London Wednesday afternoon fix at $340.15 and the New York close Tuesday around $339.70/20. Early in the session gold and silver gained on news U.S. of surge in U.S. economic growth in the first quarter which revived inflationary fears.

CBOT soft red winter wheat futures ended higher on a rally in soybeans plus follow -through technical strength from the firm tone Tuesday. Traders said the wheat market was due for a technical bounce after a recent sharp drop in the market. Export activity also was mentioned. USDA early Wednesday said U.S. exporters reported a sale of 110,000 tonnes of wheat to unknown destinations. Pakistan is slated in the market Saturday for 315,000 tonnes of U.S. or Australian white wheat. The market also remained edgy over freeze damage estimates in the U.S. hard red winter wheat crop. Wheat closed 2-1/2 to 12 cents per bushel higher, with May up 12 at $4.23.

NYMEX crude ended lower Wednesday after a top official at Venezuela's state oil company renewed his country's call for a change in the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries' (OPEC) quota system. May heating oil ended 0.84 cent a gallon lower at 58.07 cents. June crude ended 23 cents a barrel lower at $20.21.
